title: Adlai Stevenson Dresses Down the Soviet Ambassador to the UN—Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Ten
summary: The U.S. Ambassador to the United Nation delivers a victory in the courtroom of world opinion as the dangers of the Cuban Missile Crisis grow.

ai.sum: Adlai Stevenson confronted the Soviet UN ambassador during the tenth day of the Cuban Missile Crisis.

brief.summary: The piece is a historical essay by CFR's James Lindsay recounting Day Ten (25 October 1962) of the Cuban Missile Crisis. The authors describe how Kennedy's cold reply to Khrushchev offered no concessions, and how he set aside U Thant's proposal for a mutual halt to the quarantine and arms shipments because he saw it as equating the US response with the Soviet provocation. They then portray Adlai Stevenson's confrontation with Soviet UN ambassador Valerian Zorin at the Security Council, in which Stevenson demanded a yes-or-no answer on the missiles and produced photographs to expose Soviet denials. The essay argues this was a major diplomatic victory, while noting it did not resolve the core problem, since the Soviets had not withdrawn the missiles and CIA reporting that evening confirmed some were operational. The piece is retrospective and does not draw present-day policy recommendations.
brief.argument: Stevenson's public exposure of Soviet lies at the UN scored a decisive political win for the United States, though it left the underlying missile standoff unresolved.
